title: The Cloud-Sprite's Sparkle Trail
markdown:
The wind in the Craggy Peaks doesn’t blow. It sings.

It whistled through wind-bent firs like an orchestra tuning up, and it sang of sky-secrets along the grey rock. High on the mountainside, Juniper’s cottage clung like a brave patch of moss. She adjusted her spectacles. Her sigh was soft, a reedy flute on a gust.

“Honestly, Biscuit,” she said, voice like a tiny bell, “you’d think a creature made of pure light would have more sense than to nestle in the very jaws of a storm cloud.”

Biscuit the stoat, fur the colour of warm toast, eyes brighter than most professors, twitched his whiskers. “Chitter-chitter! Up there, Juniper! The very tippity-top!” He pointed a clawed paw at the highest jagged point of Mount Whispers. Snagged in a swirl of cloud: a faint pulsing shimmer, like a trapped star.

That shimmer was Glimmer, Juniper’s cloud-sprite, woven from mist and moonlight. Happy, he glowed like a sunbeam caught in a jar. His choice of nap-spot meant one thing: an adventure. Juniper did not despair. She sighed with cheerful exasperation, pulled on boots patched with leaves and mushroom leather, and reached for chamomile and a sensible plan. A sturdy rope, too, just in case. She was a witch, yes, but more wonder-working gardener and tea-brewer than spell-slinger. Her magic lived in moon-petals and sun-drops, and in the sometimes-perilous art of fetching a beloved pet down from the sky.

The path wound upward, a ribbon of grey rock and tough little flowers that dared the wind. Pine shadows striped the mountain like a giant’s charcoal drawings. The air grew thin and sharp: clean rock, damp earth. Biscuit darted ahead, sniffing pebbles, chattering encouragement. “Higher, Juniper! The wind tickles my nose like dandelion fluff!”

Around a moss-covered boulder that looked like a sleeping stone giant, they found a stall cobbled from driftwood and colourful scraps. Behind it sat Gorble the goblin trader, skin like damp soil, eyes sharp as black currants, tunic a patchwork of forgotten socks. Buttons, odd stones, a lonely boot, a dusty lute. Gorble was known for finding things others had lost — or had not yet missed.

“Well now, well now!” His voice was pebbles in a tin can. “A witch and her scurrying shadow! Looking for something to mend a tear? Light a fire? Tickle a grumpy badger?”

Juniper offered a gentle smile. “An airy companion, actually. He’s taken up residence on the highest point, and he seems quite comfortable.”

Gorble’s eyes gleamed. He rummaged, fabrics rustling like autumn leaves, and drew out a large carved bellows, dark wood etched with tiny clouds. “The Mountain’s Sigh! Blow, and you summon any breeze you wish — whisper to hearty gust. Perfect for coaxing something that’s… up there.”

It was beautiful. Heavy. Juniper traced the swirls, and a wrongness tickled her mind. Glimmer was not a thing that needed a breeze. Glimmer was sunshine and mist made alive. Biscuit, meanwhile, sniffed a pile of shimmering dust at Gorble’s feet — dust with an inner light.

“Guaranteed to move anything light and fluffy,” Gorble insisted, puffing his chest. “A wind machine for the mountainside!”

Juniper nearly took it. A bellows would be a proper tool. A plan. A haul. Then she held the carved instrument near her ear instead of her mouth, and listened.

The wind in the Craggy Peaks doesn’t blow. It sings.

She heard a hawk. Wind in the rocks. And then a faint hum — Glimmer, weak as a fading ember. Sadness. Longing.

Biscuit twitched his nose toward the shimmering dust. Juniper understood. Glimmer was not something to be pushed. Gorble’s bellows was designed to push. What Glimmer needed was to be drawn.

“Biscuit,” she said, eyes twinkling, “do you remember that pot of Starlight Dew I brewed last week? The one that makes things shine a little brighter, and smell of moonbeams and honey?”

Biscuit somersaulted. “Chitter-chitter! The sparkly stuff! It made my whiskers glow in the dark!”

She handed the bellows back. “A fine tool, Mr Gorble. But not for this particular gust.” From a leather pouch she drew a tiny corked vial, liquid pulsing with a soft inner glow: dew from moonlit spiderwebs, infused with a thousand fireflies.

“Glimmer isn’t a leaf to be blown from a tree. He’s more like a butterfly. He loves gentle light. If I sprinkle a little along the path, leading downwards, he might follow the sparkle right down to me.”

That was the slower way. The unimpressive way. She felt the cost of it as she turned from the stall: no grand machine, no hearty gust, only droplets and patience, and a goblin watching with his jaw ajar.

With Biscuit trotting beside her, nudging the vial so luminous drops fell on grey rock, Juniper began her careful descent. The dew caught sunlight, then the fading afternoon, a shimmering trail like fallen stars. On the pinnacle above, a faint warm glow appeared. Then a little more. She paused, listening. A soft happy sigh of light drifted down, like a contented dream. At last, with a whisper of mist and a joyful pulse, Glimmer descended — a swirling cascade of shimmering energy — and landed on Juniper’s outstretched hand, cool and bright against her palm.

“Oh, Glimmer. You are the most mischievous little cloud-sprite I know. You do like to keep me on my toes.”

He pulsed, wrapping her fingers like a warm shimmering scarf. Biscuit chittered, rubbing her ankles, tail flicking.

Gorble scratched his head. “Well, I’ll be a grumpy mushroom. Never thought of that. Just… shining a path. Clever. Very clever.”

The sun dipped, painting the peaks orange, rose, and violet. Juniper hummed a small tune of contentment. Glimmer pulsed on her shoulder. Biscuit, bravest stoat in the Craggy Peaks, trotted beside them, satisfied with adventure and a problem solved without a haul.

They reached the cottage that still clung like moss. Chamomile was already on the air, as if the kettle had believed they would come back the slow way. Juniper set Glimmer on the windowsill where the first stars could see him, and did not reach for the rope. She brewed the tea strong, the way she always had, and listened to the firs.

The wind in the Craggy Peaks doesn’t blow. It sings. And sometimes, if you refuse the bellows, it sings a sprite all the way home.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
